<description>
{
 "summary": "Introduces an AddrPolicy predicate callback to AddrMan::GetAddr() to filter out addresses during selection rather than post-processing. CConnman::GetAddressesUnsafe() uses this callback to skip banned and discouraged peers while populating the requested address quota. AddrMan also logs the breakdown of addresses filtered by network, quality, and policy.",
 "problem": "Previously, CConnman::GetAddressesUnsafe() fetched a target number of addresses from AddrMan and then erased banned and discouraged addresses from the result. When many banned or discouraged addresses were selected, callers like getnodeaddresses and P2P GETADDR handlers received fewer addresses than requested or none at all, even if AddrMan held plenty of valid alternatives.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: Repro: ban or discourage a large set of addresses, then call getnodeaddresses 1, previously underfilled. After this change, the RPC returns up to the requested count as expected."
 ],
 "dependencies": {
  "depends_on": [],
  "enables": []
 },
 "scope_notes": "The callback is executed inside AddrManImpl::GetAddr_ while holding AddrMan::cs, introducing a lock acquisition order of AddrMan::cs followed by BanMan::m_banned_mutex.",
 "confidence": "high"
}
</description>

<discussion_facts>
open objections:
- fjahr (member), approach, open, blocking: mixing AddrPolicy with existing network and quality parameters introduces redundant filtering mechanisms
- Bicaru20 (contributor), approach, open, blocking: introducing an AddrPolicy predicate adds unnecessary complexity compared to oversampling
- fjahr (member), approach, open, blocking: introducing AddrPolicy is overengineering compared to a simpler oversampling approach
- ajtowns (member), approach, open: filtering on selection leaves banned addresses in addrman where they compete for slots, unlike evicting them upon ban
- frankomosh (contributor), correctness, open: unit tests run with unlimited caps and fail to detect a mutant reverting the fix, leaving underfill prevention untested
support:
- mzumsande (member): Concept ACK; good to return full address sets in GetAddr responses so peers cannot deduce ban list sizes
- frankomosh (contributor): Concept ACK; 
- mzumsande (member): ACK; AddrPolicy avoids module coupling between addrman and banman despite the implied lock order
- sipa (member): Concept ACK; moving selection logic into a function argument is a reasonable direction
- frankomosh (contributor): Concept ACK; filtering during selection is a good approach
</discussion_facts>

<candidates>
<category name="p2p" title="P2P">
## Covers

Everything between this node and other nodes: connection management and
peer selection, address management, the message protocol and its
transport (including the encrypted v2 transport), block and transaction
relay including compact blocks, headers sync, transaction request and
orphan handling, network-level DoS protections, and the Tor, I2P, and
CJDNS integrations. The P2P and Private Broadcast labels are a strong
prior.

Not p2p: what the node does with a block or transaction once received
(validation, mempool); RPCs that merely report peer state (rpc).

## What matters here

Resistance to attack first: eclipse and partition resistance, DoS
resistance in message handling and resource accounting, and privacy of
transaction origin. Then relay correctness and liveness: blocks and
transactions propagate reliably and quickly, and nothing gets stuck.
Then interoperability with the rest of the network and with new
protocol features (BIPs) that other software depends on. Then bandwidth
and resource use, which node operators feel. Then connectivity across
network types and platforms.

Protocol changes with a specification and other implementations
waiting rank higher than local optimizations. Refactors count when they
retire a known hazard in message handling.

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.
